Name: Backrooms
Review:
The sound design deserves a standing ovation. Every echo, every bit of silence works in harmony with the film's liminal, and deeply unsettling atmosphere. It never relies on cheap scares, it lets the environment do the haunting.
(Hum zameen ke rehne waalon ki taraf se aapko khush-aamad-eed kehtein hai) 😰😰😰
The concept itself is so refreshingly unique that I almost consider the "confused" feelings it gives as a compliment. When a film leaves enough room for the audience to theorize, debate, and piece things together on their own, it usually means it has created a world worth thinking about. Sure, I did need a few explanation videos, but yeah that shit only made me appreciate it more. It's not a movie that hands you answers, unlike other horror movies we usually see. A genuinely interesting watch that left me wanting more. (Omw to a re-watch fs)

Name: Steins;Gate
Review:
TOO TOO ROOOOO ✨

Months ago, if someone had told me I'd end up emotionally invested in two socially awkward mad scientists flirting over *Dk Pepper* and microwaved jelly bananas, I'd have laughed.

Then Episode 12 happened.

Steins;Gate is one of those rare stories where the first half isn't really the story. It's an investment. You're forced to live with these characters, learn their quirks and behaviour, sit through their weird antics, so much so that you know exactly what a charecter would do if they were in a certain situation, and wonder when the actual plot is going to begin. And when it finally does, every seemingly insignificant moment comes back demanding emotional interest.

The emotional payoff is phenomenal. Watching Okabe slowly crumble under the weight of repeatedly choosing between the people he loves is heartbreaking, and by the finale I was rooting for two self-proclaimed mad scientists to confess harder than I've rooted for some actual romances.

That being said, I can't ignore the pacing. Spending half the runtime establishing characters felt excessive, and some episodes became so repetitive that I found myself thinking, "I get it... can we move forward now?" The washed-out, overexposed visuals also weren't for me. I understand the artistic choice or whatever, but they genuinely started giving me headaches after long viewing sessions.

Still, when Steins;Gate finally starts cashing the emotional cheques it spent twelve episodes filling in... it cashes every single one of them.

Also, I'm convinced Summertime Rendering and Steins;Gate are long-lost cousins. Different execution, different strengths, but spiritually they're cut from the same cloth.

El Psy Kongroo. 🥼⏳

Name: Oldboy
Review:
The hallway fight. I'm still wondering how they pulled it off. Maybe it's a Korean thing, or maybe it's just a coincidence that, the only movies I've watched that use still frames and move characters around happen to be Korean. Either way, I'm a sucker for scenes like that, get me more of it already. The ants foreshadowing? Caught it immediately. The moment Mi-do mentioned seeing ants, I knew there was something more to it. I guess i should spend some time touching grass. And that's where my relationship with Oldboy gets complicated. Because, at the end of the day, this film lives and dies by its shock value. It's an incredible experience to witness once, but it's also something I'd never willingly put myself through again. Knowing the answer takes away a lot of what makes it special, and that's ultimately why I can't bring myself to give it anything above a 4. As for the infamous ending people tend to argue about, I don't think the hypnosis worked on Oh Dae-su. I think human beings are simply terrified of being alone. Faced with a reality that couldn't be undone, and a love he couldn't let go of, he chose to smile and live with it.
"Smile, and the world smiles too. Weep, and you weep alone."
That final smile isn't happiness. It's acceptance. It's a coping mechanism.

Name: Main Vaapas Aaunga
Review:
"If I had a choice between leaving my home and dying, I would have gladly chosen death. Unfortunately, I did not have such a choice."
- An anonymous refugee Main Vaapas Aaunga is a film that explores the already well-known theme of love, alongside the infamous painful reality of the 1947 partition. It's a story of confrontation rather than escape, where Ishar Singh Grewal is forced to confront the past he's been carrying, through his grandson, Nirvair Grewal. It signifies that sometimes, you don't want the past back because it was perfect, you want it back because that's where you remember being whole, that's where you remember being yourself. Imtiaz Ali's recurring obsession with longing, is particularly interesting, and has been portrayed beautifully in this film, thanks to Naseeruddin Shah, and Diljit Dosanjh. Their characters were both, executed so well, that they capture the exact feeling Imtiaz Ali was aiming for. A story of Memories, lost love, displacement, belonging, and longing, for me personally, is an absolute masterpiece.

Name: Barakamon
Review:
"You're sure gonna miss them, will you not?" "Actually, I'm looking forward to the next time I'd see them."
Barakamon is a story about finding life in places you never intended to stay. After making an impulsive attempt to escape from the aftermath of his own impulses, Handa Seishuu is encountered with a life that he never knew he needed. There's something incredibly beautiful about the way Barakamon portrays family. Handa arrives on the island to seek solitude, to understand his art, and to hone his craft. He arrives with sheer pride, and excessive narcissistic traits, only to understand that everything he creates, learns, and eventually understands, comes from the people constantly interrupting this solitude he's been seeking. Everything slowly becomes a part of him so deep, he refuses to now let go of them. And perhaps, that's exactly why I love this show. Barakamon doesn't romanticise some huge ass escape from life or some crazy ass vacation. It romanticises actually living the life yourself, and discovering your own self, and letting others discover themselves, just like Handa Seishuu trying to find himself only to end up finding people. One of those rare gems you curiously click play on, at 2 AM, only to keep going until you finish it off and there's no season 2, just you and your now changed perspective of life. Beautiful, Funny, Warm, and Unexpectedly Lovable. An absolute Masterpiece.

Masaan is a very grounded, unique, and beautiful piece of cinema. Starting off with the cinematography, I personally am a sucker for such shots and such unique grading. Then the acting, doesn't disappoint even a bit, each character is portrayed amazingly. The Charecters themselves are so well written, each one has a sophisticated way they function and they stay true to it throughout. Nothing in this film feels out of place. Although, it does become a bit predictable by the end, but that's the beauty of Masaan. Even after that, leaves you struck with Awe, and it feels like a shot of depression right into your veins, and I LOVE my movies like that.
